arctic-small-tool-tradition.name: Arctic Small Tool tradition
arctic-small-tool-tradition.summary: A prehistoric culture that arose around Alaska and the Bering Strait about 2500 BC, marked by a microblade toolkit, whose people were the first to settle Arctic Canada and Greenland.

magnetic-island-alaska.name: Magnetic Island
magnetic-island-alaska.summary: A small island in Cook Inlet, Alaska, named for local magnetism and the site of a prehistoric habitation dated to about 1800-1400 BCE, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

cook-inlet.name: Cook Inlet
cook-inlet.summary: A 180-mile inlet in south-central Alaska stretching from the Gulf of Alaska to Anchorage, fed by many rivers and glaciers and known for strong tidal currents.

rock-carvings-at-alta.name: Alta
rock-carvings-at-alta.summary: Municipality in northern Norway with over 6,000 rock carvings dated from about 4200 to 500 BCE, showing a hunter-gatherer culture skilled in reindeer herding and boat building.

devon-island.name: Devon Island
devon-island.summary: The world's largest uninhabited island, in Canada's Arctic Archipelago, notable for its Mars-like surface and the Haughton impact crater.

paleo-eskimo.name: Paleo-Eskimo
paleo-eskimo.summary: The peoples who inhabited the Arctic from Siberia to Greenland before the modern Inuit, with cultures developing from about 3900 BCE and the last, the Dorset, disappearing around 1500 CE.

peary-land.name: Peary Land
peary-land.summary: A peninsula in northern Greenland extending into the Arctic Ocean, reaching from Victoria Fjord to Independence Fjord and containing Cape Morris Jesup, Greenland's northernmost point.

independence-fjord.name: Independence Fjord
independence-fjord.summary: A roughly 200 km long fjord in northern Greenland, after which two ancient Paleo-Eskimo cultures were later named.

independence-i-culture.name: Independence I culture
independence-i-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture that lived in northern Greenland and the Canadian Arctic from about 2400 to 1900 BC, among the earliest known cultures in Greenland.

saqqaq-culture.name: Saqqaq culture
saqqaq-culture.summary: A Paleo-Inuit culture in southern Greenland, named after the settlement of Saqqaq, and the longest-residing culture in Greenland's history.

pre-dorset.name: Pre-Dorset
pre-dorset.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture, or group of cultures, in the Eastern Canadian Arctic from about 3200 to 850 BCE that preceded the Dorset culture.

dorset-culture.name: Dorset culture
dorset-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture in the North American Arctic, lasting from about 500 BCE until it died out by 1000–1500 CE, before the Thule (proto-Inuit) arrived. Inuit legends recall its people as the Tuniit.

sisimiut.name: Sisimiut
sisimiut.summary: The second-largest city in Greenland, settled for about 4,500 years by the Saqqaq, Dorset and Thule peoples before Danish settlement in the 1720s.

thule-people.name: Thule people
thule-people.summary: The precursors of modern Inuit and Yupik peoples, who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE, spread across the Arctic, and replaced the earlier Dorset culture by the 15th century.

nares-strait.name: Nares Strait
nares-strait.summary: A waterway between Ellesmere Island and Greenland linking Baffin Bay to the Lincoln Sea, known for hazardous ice conditions and named after naval officer George Strong Nares.

qeqertarsuaq.name: Qeqertarsuaq
qeqertarsuaq.summary: A port town founded in 1773 on Disko Island in western Greenland, and also the Kalaallisut name for the island itself, meaning 'the big island.'

disko-island.name: Disko Island
disko-island.summary: Large island off western Greenland, the second-largest island belonging to Greenland and among the world's 100 largest islands.

kalaallit.name: Kalaallit
kalaallit.summary: The largest indigenous group in Greenland, part of the Inuit people, whose language, Kalaallisut, is known in English as Greenlandic.

chukchi-people.name: Chukchi
chukchi-people.summary: A Siberian ethnic group native to the Chukchi Peninsula and nearby Arctic coasts, genetically the closest Asian relatives of Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

koryaks.name: Koryaks
koryaks.summary: Indigenous people of the Russian Far East living north of the Kamchatka Peninsula along the Bering Sea coast, split between coastal fishing communities and inland reindeer herders; about 7,953 recorded in Russia in 2010.
